title: Scoreboard Engineer
objectives: I can create a variable and explain that it stores a value that can change.
I can use a variable to build a working score counter.
I can test my scoring code across several rounds to check it is actually right.
I can use a forever loop to keep my scoreboard on screen, and say how a loop is different from an event.

config.headline: Every game keeps score. Today you build the scorekeeper.
lines: In this lesson you will learn what a VARIABLE is — a named box in the computer's memory that holds a number, where the name stays the same but the number can change. It is the single most useful idea in all of programming, and by the end of the hour you will have built one, changed it, reset it and watched it work.
Look at the photos: the arcade's high-score table, a GAA scoreboard, the step count on a wrist. Behind every one is a variable — a box called score, or steps, holding a number that moves.

You will also learn the second SHAPE of code. Lesson 2 was all events — code that waits for a press. Today you add the LOOP: code that never stops. Your scoreboard uses both at once, and knowing which job belongs to which is the real lesson.

And at the end, your scoreboard gets a real job: a whole-class Reaction Rally, scored on the machines you built. You are secretly on a team — nobody finds out who is with who until the reveal at the very end.

config.title: The Scoreboard Ladder
config.intro:
This is where you build it — with the person beside you, one micro:bit shared between the two of you. Three rungs, each one an upgrade, and the micro:bit is the judge: the number on the LED grid is either right or it's lying.

You BOTH build every rung, each on your OWN computer — exactly like last lesson. Talk it through together as you go, and watch the simulator on your own screen: it shows your score the moment your blocks change. You share the real micro:bit for the real test, so take turns: at each rung, one of you downloads the program and drags the file across while the other presses the buttons and reads the display. Swap over at every rung, so you both do both.

You'll build TWO shapes of code today: an EVENT that sits and waits to be triggered, and a LOOP that just keeps going on its own.
config.setupLead: Before rung 1, set MakeCode up like this:
setup: Open MakeCode using the button above. Keep it in its own tab all lesson.

Click New Project, type scoreboard as the project's name, and press Create. Do NOT open your Signal Relay project from last lesson — today's scoreboard is a fresh build. (Missed the name box? Click the box at the bottom that says Untitled and type scoreboard there.)
A blue Welcome box may pop up when the editor opens — click its ✕ to close it. You do not need the tour today.
Build all three rungs in this SAME project. It grows as you climb — you never start another one today.

Every time you press Download it saves a new copy of the WHOLE project, replacing the one from last time. If a box asks whether you want to replace the old file, say yes — that is exactly what you want.

rungs.title: Rung 1 — Wake the Scoreboard
rungs.target: Your challenge: wake the scoreboard. Build exactly what Part 2 showed you: 1. make a variable called score — 2. put 'show number score' INSIDE the forever block that is already sitting on your canvas.
rungs.imgAlt: The finished blocks for rung 1: a forever block with 'show number score' inside it.
rungs.test: Watch your simulator, without pressing anything: it already reads 0. Nobody pressed a button — the forever loop starts by itself and shows the number in the box, over and over. Now copy it onto the micro:bit the same way as last lesson: press Download in MakeCode, then drag the file across onto the MICROBIT drive. (If your micro:bit won't connect, the on-screen simulator counts while your teacher sorts it.) The real display reads 0 too — your scoreboard is awake.
rungs.hint: Variables → 'Make a Variable...' → name it score. Do NOT drag a new forever block: every new project already has one (next to 'on start'). From Basic drag 'show number 0' into forever's mouth, then drop the round 'score' block from Variables into the 0 slot so it reads 'show number score'.

rungs.title: Rung 2 — Make It Count
rungs.target: Your challenge: make every press of button A count. Build what Part 3 showed you: 1. add a separate event: 'on button A pressed' with 'set score to 1' inside — press A on the simulator a few times and watch it stick at 1 — 2. now swap 'set score to 1' for 'change score by 1'. When you're done, your button A event holds just that one block — the loop is still doing all the showing.
rungs.test: Download it and drag the new file across — your micro:bit keeps running the OLD program until a new file lands on it. Then press A three times. Does the number climb by exactly one per press — 1, 2, 3? One more proof, on the SIMULATOR: drag 'show number score' OUT of forever and drop it on empty canvas. The simulator's display goes dark and STAYS dark, even when you press its A — no loop, no scoreboard. Put the block back INSIDE forever. (Your real micro:bit still shows the old copy — it only changes when you download again.)
rungs.hint: Number stuck at 1 on the micro:bit? First check you downloaded again after the swap — the micro:bit only changes when a new file lands on it. Still stuck after a fresh download? Then the old 'set score to 1' block is still in there — swap it out, don't stack them: 'change score by 1' ADDS one to whatever is in the box.

rungs.title: Rung 3 — The Reset Button

part.label: Part 4 — Reset for a fresh game

rungs.target: Your challenge: give your scoreboard a fresh-start button. Add a second event: on button B pressed → set score to 0. When it works, this is what you'll have: 1. A still counts up — 2. B wipes the score back to 0 — 3. the loop keeps the number on screen the whole time.
rungs.test: Download and drag the new file across once more, so the micro:bit holds all three blocks. Then THE MULTI-ROUND TEST: press B (it says 0), press A three times (it says 3), press B (back to 0). Now run that whole cycle three times over. A scoreboard that's right once can still be wrong — three clean rounds is proof.
rungs.hint: Reset lives on its OWN event: a separate 'on button B pressed' block with 'set score to 0' inside it. You do NOT need another 'show number score' anywhere — the forever loop already shows every change the moment it happens. Leave your button A blocks alone.

stretch.title: Stretch — The High-Score Keeper
stretch.target: Your stretch challenge: teach your micro:bit to REMEMBER the best score ever. Build it in three steps: 1. make a SECOND variable called highScore — 2. add: on shake → if score > highScore then set highScore to score — 3. teach the loop to show both: inside forever, after 'show number score', add pause (ms) 1000 → show string "H" → show number highScore → pause (ms) 1000.
stretch.test: Score 3 and shake — after the H you see 3. Score 5, shake — after the H you see 5. Now score just 2 and shake — after the H it STILL says 5? Then your micro:bit officially remembers the best. That 'if' block is asking a question — next lesson runs on them.

Three rungs, each one an upgrade, and the micro:bit is the judge (or the on-screen simulator). config.title: The Reaction Rally
config.intro: Your scoreboard's first real job. You are secretly on a team — nobody knows who's with who until the final reveal. Every point you bank is banked for your hidden team.
rules: A rally round: the REFEREE holds the micro:bit where you both can see it, and gives 10 surprise signals — a sharp "NOW!" whenever they like.
The PLAYER hovers over button A. On each "NOW!", the referee calls it: "CATCH!" for a fast reaction, "MISS!" for a slow one. The referee's word is final.
CATCH means the player presses A — the scoreboard they built counts it. MISS means hands off: no press, no point.
Round 1: one of you plays. Round 2: swap jobs. Round 3: the pair chooses — whoever is doing better today plays the last round (real teams choose who finishes).

Press B for a fresh 0 before every round. At the end of a round, read the final number OFF the micro:bit's display and enter exactly that number below with the + and − buttons — your pair's BEST round is the one that counts.
config.confirm: We ran the multi-round test first — B to zero, count up, B to zero, three times, no lies
config.soloIntro: The live Rally happened in class — but your scoreboard still gets its moment. Your catch-up job: prove your rig is tournament-grade, then log your best solo round.
soloRules: Run the multi-round test: B to zero, three presses, B to zero — three full cycles, no lies on the display.
Now a solo round: 10 self-signals — say "now" in your head at random moments, press A only on a genuinely clean reaction. Referee yourself honestly.
Play three rounds, pressing B for a fresh 0 each time. Read each round's final number off the micro:bit's display and enter it below — your best round still counts for your hidden team.
config.soloConfirm: I ran the multi-round test three times — the scoreboard never lied

suspense.sealed: Teams are SEALED. Nobody in this room knows who they're carrying points for.

config.intro: Three scenarios before you go — and these ARE marked: your teacher sees how the class did. Think like a scoreboard engineer.

items.stem: In the Rally, a pair press button A five times — five clean catches — but the display says 1 after every single press. What's the MOST likely cause?
options: Their event still has 'set score to 1' inside it instead of 'change score by 1'
The LED display can only show the number 1
They pressed the button too fast

items.stem: A program runs 'set score to 0'. Then 'change score by 1' runs twice. What does 'show number score' display?
Halfway through a rally, the variable named score holds 7. Which sentence is TRUE?
options: The word 'score' will always mean 7 from now on
score currently holds 7 — the very next catch can change it
The program now has seven different scores
7 has become the program's name for score

config.help: Three marked questions about today. Answer on your own — your verdicts arrive once the whole report is filed, at the end of the last screen.

config.intro: Last one: four real blocks, two jobs, one working scoreboard. Put them in the order the sentence describes — the loop's job and the event's job.

item.prompt: Your scoreboard has two jobs. The first keeps the current score on the LEDs all by itself, over and over, showing whatever number is in the box. The second waits for button A, and adds one to that number every time it is pressed.

config.help: Click blocks from the tray into your program, in the order the sentence describes. Check when you're sure — you'll be shown the working order if it's off.
